section_summary: This section combines routine corporate shipment reports and State Department acknowledgments with congressional and private correspondence urging restrictions on exports of strategic materials to Japan. Its centerpiece is the illustrated April 1940 pamphlet “Shall America Stop Arming Japan?”, which argues that American petroleum, metals, machinery, vehicles, and trade finance were sustaining Japanese aggression in China and advocates embargo legislation and import restrictions. The concluding correspondence concerns criticism of broader U.S. foreign policy, a Soviet complaint about unequal application of the moral embargo, requests for export statistics, and Ford Motor Company’s denial that it had sold vehicles to Japan.

subfiles.title: Petroleum exports to selected markets, 1920–1938 (continuation)
subfiles.about: Continuation of a statistical table comparing the value and quantity of a petroleum commodity shipped to Japan, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom, and Canada.
subfiles.summary: The page continues a multi-year table covering 1920–1938, with columns for value and quantities measured in 42-gallon barrels. The commodity heading is truncated, but the data compare four foreign markets and clearly belong to a document begun on an earlier page.

subfiles.title: No April shipments of ethyl fluid to Japan or Russia
subfiles.from: J. Goux, Associated Ethyl Company Limited
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, attention Charles W. Yost
subfiles.about: Reports that the company made no shipments to Japan or Russia during April 1940.
subfiles.summary: J. Goux responds to a State Department request for monthly shipment information. He states that the Associated Ethyl Company Limited made no April shipments to either Japan or Russia.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Associated Ethyl Company report
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the report that no ethyl fluid was shipped to Japan or the Soviet Union in April.
subfiles.summary: Yost thanks Goux for the May 1 report. He restates that the company made no April shipments of ethyl fluid to Japan or the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics.

subfiles.title: Phillips Petroleum report of propane delivered for export to Japan
subfiles.from: K. S. Adams, Phillips Petroleum Company
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, attention Joseph C. Green
subfiles.about: Reports the April delivery of 32,170 gallons of propane to Mitsui & Co. for export to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Adams submits the monthly report requested by the Department in January. Phillips Petroleum delivered 32,170 gallons of propane to Mitsui & Co., Ltd., during April for export to Japan.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Phillips Petroleum propane report
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Phillips Petroleum’s report of propane supplied to Mitsui for export to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges Adams’s May 1 letter concerning the April propane delivery. The OCR renders the amount imperfectly, but the acknowledgment plainly refers to the shipment reported on the preceding page.

subfiles.title: Senator Lucas requests comment on A. C. Moore’s scrap-export letter
subfiles.about: Forwards a letter from A. C. Moore and asks for the Department’s reaction.
subfiles.summary: Senator Lucas sends the Department correspondence from the president of the Chicago Railway Equipment Company. He requests the Department’s views on Moore’s arguments concerning exports of iron and steel scrap.

subfiles.title: A. C. Moore urges controls on iron and steel scrap exports
subfiles.about: Argues that Congress should restrict scrap exports because they weaken American industry and defense while aiding foreign military power.
subfiles.summary: Moore encloses a Chicago newspaper editorial and renews his criticism of unrestricted iron and steel scrap exports. He contends that conserving scrap is economically prudent and essential to national defense, and compares congressional inaction to Nero fiddling while Rome burned.

subfiles.title: “Scrap for What Scrap?”
subfiles.about: Warns that American iron and steel scrap could be transformed into Japanese warships and used against the United States.
subfiles.summary: The editorial notes large American scrap inventories but argues that much of this material may eventually become naval tonnage for Japan. It claims Japan depends on American scrap for shipbuilding and condemns public and congressional complacency toward exports that could later endanger American ships and servicemen.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Senator Lucas on scrap exports
subfiles.about: Explains that no existing statute authorizes the proposed embargo on scrap exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledges Lucas’s letter transmitting A. C. Moore’s protest and editorial. He explains that the Department generally appreciates such views but that the government presently lacks statutory authority to impose the requested embargo. New legislation would therefore be required, and Moore’s materials are returned.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck memorandum on Price correspondence and pamphlet
subfiles.about: Calls Welles’s attention to passages marked by Hornbeck and Alger Hiss in the enclosed anti-armament pamphlet.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck refers to correspondence with Harry B. Price and suggests that Welles inspect the attached booklet. He notes that he and Alger Hiss have marked selected passages for attention.

subfiles.title: Welles requests a draft reply to Price
subfiles.about: Requests that Hornbeck’s division prepare a reply for Welles’s signature.
subfiles.summary: Welles routes the Price correspondence to Hornbeck. He asks the division to draft an appropriate reply for his signature.

subfiles.title: Price transmits “Shall America Stop Arming Japan?”
subfiles.about: Sends the American Committee’s newly published illustrated booklet opposing American material support for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Price forwards the pamphlet “Shall America Stop Arming Japan?” to the Under Secretary of State. He expresses hope that Welles will examine it and find its presentation of the issue fair.

subfiles.title: Welles acknowledges Price’s pamphlet
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of the booklet and promises to examine it carefully.
subfiles.summary: Welles thanks Price for the April 29 letter and enclosed pamphlet. He assures Price that he will carefully examine the booklet’s contents.

subfiles.title: “Shall America Stop Arming Japan?”
subfiles.from: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: Argues for ending American exports and economic support that enabled Japan’s war in China.
subfiles.summary: The pamphlet traces Japanese territorial expansion, the invasion of China, and the history of the Open Door policy and Nine Power Treaty. Through maps, charts, quotations, cartoons, trade statistics, and press excerpts, it contends that Japan depended heavily on American petroleum, scrap metal, copper, machinery, vehicles, and markets to sustain its military campaign. It argues that withholding war supplies and restricting Japanese imports would favor Chinese independence without posing a substantial risk of war with the United States. The concluding sections endorse embargo legislation, executive tariff action, postwar reconstruction, and economic cooperation as foundations for an enduring Pacific peace.

subfiles.title: Hyslop challenges Hornbeck on exports to Japan and other foreign-policy issues
subfiles.about: Demands a specific defense of U.S. policies permitting strategic exports to Japan and raises related complaints about credits to Franco and tin shipments to Russia.
subfiles.summary: Hyslop argues that permitting exports of scrap iron, copper, cotton, oil, tin, and machinery to Japan is economically, ethically, and socially indefensible. Quoting Samuel Grafton, he says the United States strengthens Japan militarily and then spends heavily on defenses against it. He also criticizes a reported American credit for Franco’s Spain and shipments of tin to Russia, and says he intends to question Senator Pittman about Japanese trade negotiations and the proposed Spanish loan.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck acknowledges Hyslop’s foreign-policy letter
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Hyslop’s further criticism of U.S. foreign policy and promises to circulate his comments.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck says he has read Hyslop’s May 11 letter with interest. He promises to bring its comments to the attention of other Department officials.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to memorandum on Soviet Ambassador Umansky and the moral embargo
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of European Affairs
subfiles.about: References a memorandum recording the Soviet ambassador’s complaint about application of the moral embargo to the Soviet Union and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet points to an April 9 memorandum about a conversation with Soviet Ambassador Konstantin Umansky. Umansky asserted that moral embargoes were applied equally to the Soviet Union and Japan, while claiming that aircraft and parts continued to reach Japan for months after the embargo was announced.

subfiles.title: Representative Johnson forwards an inquiry about exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Requests available information in response to an enclosed constituent inquiry concerning shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Johnson forwards a letter asking about exports to Japan. He asks Moore to supply the requested information if available and to return the enclosure with the reply.

subfiles.title: William Ives requests statistics and action on exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Requests export values for gasoline, scrap iron, fuel oil, lubricating oil, and machine tools sent to Japan and asks what Johnson is doing to stop them.
subfiles.summary: Ives asks for the value of selected strategic exports to Japan during 1939 and 1940 to date. He characterizes these materials as being used destructively against the Chinese people and requests a report on Johnson’s legislative record concerning the trade.

subfiles.title: Moore replies to Johnson on Ives’s request
subfiles.about: Explains that the Commerce Department maintains the requested statistics and reiterates the lack of statutory authority for an embargo.
subfiles.summary: Moore notes that the State Department received an identical letter directly from Ives and forwarded it to the Department of Commerce for statistical reply. He also repeats that no existing statute authorizes the requested embargo on war materials to Japan and that new legislation would be needed. Ives’s letter is returned to Johnson.

subfiles.title: Greene forwards Ford correspondence
subfiles.to: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Department of State
subfiles.about: Sends a copy of a Ford Motor Company letter that may contain information absent from official reports.
subfiles.summary: Greene calls attention to a letter concerning Ford vehicles in Japan and China. Believing that it may add details not contained in official reports, he supplies a copy to the Department.

subfiles.title: Ford Motor Company denies selling vehicles to Japan
subfiles.from: W. J. Cameron, Ford Motor Company
subfiles.about: States that Ford sold nothing to Japan and explains that its Japanese plant and dealer stocks had been taken over.
subfiles.summary: Cameron rejects accusations that Ford supplied Japan with vehicles for use against China. He says the company’s Japanese plant and dealer inventories were taken over after Henry Ford refused a proposed partnership with the Japanese government, while Japanese authorities called away Ford personnel and unsuccessfully attempted to operate the plant. He adds that Chinese forces maintained more Ford units through French suppliers and concludes categorically that Ford had sold nothing to Japan.

subfiles.title: Hamilton acknowledges Greene’s Ford enclosure
subfiles.about: Thanks Greene for providing the copy of Cameron’s letter to Sheldon.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton acknowledges Greene’s May 13 covering letter and the enclosed April 10 Ford Motor Company correspondence. He expresses appreciation for Greene’s courtesy in supplying the material.
